title: The Hangman of Nuremberg
narrativeQuestion: What can the records prove about John C. Woods and the Nuremberg executions, and does lawful justice require humane punishment?

chapters.title: The Choice
chapters.claim: A public trial created an evidentiary record where immediate punishment would not.

chapters.title: The Verdict
chapters.claim: Of twelve death sentences, ten were carried out; Göring died by suicide and Bormann was absent.

namedPeople.name: Hermann Göring
namedPeople.role: convicted Nazi leader who died by suicide before his execution

chapters.title: The Résumé
chapters.claim: Military historian MacLean's record-based estimate diverges from Woods's self-promoted credentials.

chapters.title: The Witness
chapters.claim: The correspondent heard sounds from behind the screen but could not observe their cause.

chapters.title: The Claims
chapters.claim: Some claims are documented, others attributed or not established; those categories are different.

chapters.title: The Ending
chapters.claim: Woods died in an electrical accident in 1950, not a proven murder conspiracy.

namedPeople.name: John C. Woods
namedPeople.role: executed Nazi leaders and died on Eniwetok

chapters.title: Your Verdict
chapters.claim: The evidence for possible mishandling does not automatically establish deliberate suffering.

accuracyNotes: Never conflate Nazi defendants' guilt with disputed conduct during punishment.
Classify Woods's claim of 347 as attributed, not his verified count.
French L. MacLean's 60–100 estimate is not a formal execution count.
Witness reported sounds but could not directly identify cause or length of conscious suffering behind the screen.
Do not present 18–28-minute claims as proven.
The electrical death of Woods is documented; conspiratorial murder theories are unsubstantiated.
Local SVGs are openly identified as modern interpretations; original historical images are linked from source notes.
